title: The Most Important Factory in America by Dan Wang in NYT 23 Oct 2026
author: Xebec
text:
user nl
Well-known member

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is the world’s most advanced chipmaker. It is the company that Apple and Nvidia turn to for the most complex components of their most intricate technologies. That skill has propelled TSMC’s market cap to $2 trillion. It might be worth even more if TSMC didn’t manufacture nearly all of its chips in Taiwan, the nation that China’s Communist Party has long coveted. When typically bullish investment banks imagine a war over the island, they reach for words like “global economic depression,” “trillions in losses,” and, sometimes, “World War III.”

In 2020, TSMC announced it would build a semiconductor production facility in Arizona. It was lured by proximity to its American customers, the carrot of federal subsidies and unsubtle political pressure from the Trump administration, which has, correctly, touted the effort as the largest ever foreign direct investment into the United States. In July, TSMC announced its intention to invest a total of more than a quarter of a trillion dollars for 10 chip production plants, two packaging facilities and a research and development site, all in Arizona. TSMC now employs over 3,500 people in the state, including skilled Taiwanese engineers on temporary visas. This month, TSMC’s C.E.O. said that the company is exploring an investment in Texas.

The United States invented the semiconductor, the tiny computer processor that powered the digital age, and its biggest firms dominated the industry for decades. Then chipmakers like Intel and Texas Instruments fell behind. The hardware powering the A.I. boom is now made mostly in East Asia.

TSMC Arizona is rebuilding America’s manufacturing backbone by teaching Americans the skills that they have lost, just as the speaker at the Northwest Chinese Baptist Church predicted. For the most important asset TSMC offers is not money, equipment or local employment, but what’s known as process knowledge. The United States doesn’t lack capital. American companies are flush with cash and can conjure marvelous funds to chase new technologies. It doesn’t lack the ability to buy advanced tooling either. What America really lacks is skill: the practice of building semiconductors, automobiles, electronics and many other industries in which U.S. firms used to lead the world.
